summary: Proposes mechanisms that let Realm Specific IP work with end-to-end IPsec. Because IPsec protects packets in ways that address translation tends to break, the memo describes how an RSIP host can still use it. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network gives several private computers the same public address, the address alone cannot say which computer is sending. That breaks encrypted sessions, because the far end uses the address to recognise its partner. RFC 3104 adds two ways to tell them apart: a random cookie carried inside the key exchange, and a number that identifies each protected flow. The result is that the shared address can carry a fully encrypted session end to end.

questions: how does rsip work with ipsec
how does address translation break encryption
can you use rsip and ipsec together
subtitle: How a host behind a shared public address can still run an end-to-end encrypted session.

tldr.problem: When a server lends the same public address to several private hosts, the address no longer says which host is talking, which is a problem for IPsec, where the peer identifies its partner partly by address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the RSIP protocol with two assignment messages that hand the client an address and its own SPI values, and it matches IKE and IPsec flows by an Initiator Cookie and an SPI rather than by address alone.
tldr.outcome: Several private hosts can share one public address and still use end-to-end IPsec, but only with RSIP-aware and IPsec-aware software on both sides. The document is Experimental.

today: RFC 3104 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It belongs to a set of three: the framework is in RFC 3102, the protocol is in RFC 3103, and this memo adds IPsec support to them. The IESG note at the top of the document records the concern that the RSIP set implies significant host and gateway changes, and that its costs and benefits should be weighed against other ways of relieving address shortage.

sections.title: What the RFC Proposes
sections.content:
RFC 3104 specifies extensions to Realm Specific IP (RSIP) that enable end-to-end IPsec. It assumes the RSIP framework presented in RFC 3102 and specifies extensions to the RSIP protocol defined in RFC 3103.

The difficulty it addresses is visible in the model the document sets out. The RSIP server holds addresses in two spaces and can lend addresses from the public one to clients on a private network. A host in the public space that is not RSIP-aware but is IPsec-aware sees the IKE packets of such a client arriving from the server's public address. When the same public address is shared by several clients, the address no longer says which client is talking, and the encrypted session has no way to tell them apart. The extensions proposed here let a client run an end-to-end IPsec session with such a host regardless.

The IESG note in the memo warns that the set of documents describing RSIP implies significant host and gateway changes for a complete implementation, that the floating of port numbers can stop an RSIP-enabled host from interoperating transparently with existing applications, and that there are significant operational complexities. It says the costs and benefits of using RSIP should be carefully weighed against other means of relieving address shortage.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo adds the missing pieces that let a private computer run an encrypted session with a public server, even when several private computers share one public address. The pieces are a random number inside the key exchange and a per-flow identifier for the encrypted traffic.

sections.title: The RSIP Model
sections.content:
Hosts X and Y belong to different address spaces, A and B. The RSIP server N has two addresses: Na on space A and Nb on space B. Space A could be a private address space and space B the public address space of the general Internet. The server may also hold a pool of addresses in space B that it can assign or lend to X.

The proposed extensions let an RSIP client X start IKE and IPsec sessions with a legacy node Y that knows IKE and IPsec but nothing about RSIP. X does this by exchanging RSIP protocol messages with N. The document does not address the reverse case, in which Y initiates the session towards an RSIP client; Appendix G sets out some thoughts on that.

The document assumes the RSAP-IP flavour of RSIP, except that port number assignments are optional, and it uses SPI values on top of that for demultiplexing. Because of this, more than one RSIP client may share the same global IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture is simple: a client on a private network, a server that has one address on the private side and another on the public side, and a public host that knows nothing about the arrangement. The client borrows a public address from the server and then talks to the public host through it.

sections.title: IKE Handling and Demultiplexing
sections.content:
If an RSIP client must use port 500 as the source of its IKE traffic, that field cannot be used to tell flows apart. The Initiator Cookie field in the IKE header has to be used instead. It is guaranteed to be present in every IKE exchange, in Phase 1 and Phase 2, and to be in the clear even when later IKE payloads are encrypted, although IKE protects it with the Hash payload. The client and the server must therefore agree on a valid value for the Initiator Cookie.

Once they agree, the client uses the cookie to build an IKE packet and tunnels it to the RSIP server, which decapsulates it and sends it on address space B. The minimum tuple negotiated through RSIP, and used to match incoming IKE responses from Y at the server, is the IKE destination port number, the Initiator Cookie and the destination IP address.

One problem remains. Y is not RSIP-aware but is IKE-aware, and it sees the packets arriving from the server's public address. To stop Y from taking the source address as the identity of its IKE peer, the client must exchange client identifiers with Y: the initiator identifiers in Phase 1 and the child identifiers in Phase 2.

Section 6.1 gives two ways to reach a cookie value that is unique. The client can try one at random and watch whether the server drops the packet, or the two can negotiate one through an extension of the RSIP protocol. The memo prefers the first. The 64-bit cookie space makes a collision infinitesimal, and even by the birthday paradox a population of 640 million clients going through the same server gives a first-collision chance of just 1%. An RSIP-aware IKE client should use a different cookie for each retransmission, and IKE retransmits a lost packet at least three times.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and the server agree on a random number called the Initiator Cookie, and the client puts it in every key exchange message. The server uses it to recognise which client a message belongs to, and the client tells the far end its real identity separately, so the far end does not mistake the shared address for the partner.

sections.title: IPsec Handling and Demultiplexing
sections.content:
The client and the server must arrive at an SPI value that denotes the incoming IPsec security association from Y to X. Once the server and the client have made sure the SPI is unique within both of their SPI spaces, the client communicates its value to Y as part of establishing the security association, in Quick Mode in IKE or by manual assignment. That is what allows Y to send its IPsec packets to the client through the server's public address using the negotiated SPI.

The IPsec packets themselves arrive at the server and are matched on three fields: the protocol, which is 50 for ESP or 51 for AH; the SPI; and the destination IP address. If the server finds a matching mapping it tunnels the packet to the client according to the tunneling mode in effect. If it cannot find one, it must discard the packet.

Two consequences follow. IPsec implementations have to be aware of RSIP at least in a peripheral sense, in order to receive assigned SPIs and perhaps other parameters, so bump-in-the-stack implementations of IPsec are not expected to work out of the box with RSIP. And because the security association key is negotiated rather than derived from the address, the peer Y should not be configured to use address-based keying: with several clients sharing one public address, address-based keying would allow only one client at a time to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and the server also agree on a number that identifies one protected flow, called the SPI. The server matches incoming encrypted packets on the protocol number, that number and the destination address, and forwards the packet to the right client. A packet that matches nothing is thrown away.

sections.title: Requesting an Address and SPIs
sections.content:
The RSIP protocol is extended with two message types, ASSIGN_REQUEST_RSIPSEC and ASSIGN_RESPONSE_RSIPSEC, used when a client asks for the parameters it needs. A client must request an IP address and SPIs in one message. If it wants to protect a TCP or UDP application with IPsec, it must use the port range parameter; otherwise it must set the port parameters to the "don't need" value, which means a length field of 0 with both the number field and the port field omitted.

The client may initialise the SPI parameter to the "don't care" value, asking the server to assign a valid one, or to a value it considers valid, which is then a suggestion the server may reject. The server answers with an error if the client is not allowed to use IPsec through it, if no SPI at all can be allocated, or if the requested address and SPI tuple is already in use. The three error values are 401 IPSEC_UNALLOWED, 402 IPSEC_SPI_UNAVAILABLE and 403 IPSEC_SPI_INUSE.

A new RSIP parameter, the SPI, carries a code of 22, a length field of 2, a two-byte number field and one or more four-byte SPI values. A "don't care" request is made by setting the length field to 2, setting the number field to the number of SPIs needed and omitting the SPI fields. A server that implements this may advertise the RSIP method "RSIP with IPsec (RSIPSEC)" in its REGISTER_RESPONSE, a method assigned the value 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the server for an address and for its own flow identifiers in a single message, and the server answers with the same parameters plus a lease time. If the server cannot meet the request, it replies with one of three defined error values instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds no security issues to those already posed by NAT or by normal routing operations. Routing decisions are usually based on a tuple with only one element, the destination IP address, and this document simply adds more elements to that tuple. By allowing an end-to-end mode of operation and by introducing a negotiation phase to address reuse, the mechanisms described here are more secure and less arbitrary than NAT.

One caution is in order. SPI values are meant to be semi-random and also serve as anti-clogging tokens that reduce off-the-path denial-of-service attacks. RSIP support for IPsec makes the SPI a negotiated item: in addition to being unique values at the receiver, they must also be unique at the RSIP server. Limiting the range of SPI values available to the RSIP clients reduces their entropy slightly.

Two operational limits are worth knowing. Appendix D notes that an RSIP server may not be able to enforce local or remote micro-flow policy when a client uses ESP for end-to-end encryption, since all TCP and UDP port numbers will be encrypted, although micro-flow policy is enforceable if AH without ESP is used and macro-flow policy is always enforceable. Appendix E notes that rekeying is only an issue for RSIP when the client uses IKE port 500 and the rekey is of the ISAKMP phase 1 security association, because the remote host then sends IKE packets to port 500 with a new initiator cookie that the server has no mapping for and should drop.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo argues that this design is no less safe than ordinary routing and in some ways safer, because the flow identifiers are negotiated rather than guessed from an address. It does warn that sharing one public address between several clients means the server cannot see the port numbers inside an encrypted packet, so it cannot enforce rules at that level.
